subject: AI & Agents
title: Watson Wins Jeopardy!
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Watson Wins Jeopardy!.

hook.text: In 2011, an IBM computer faced Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. It crushed them both.

buildup.text: Watson combined natural language processing, information retrieval, and confidence scoring.

discovery.text: It parsed tricky clues with puns, wordplay, and cultural references — Jeopardy!'s signature difficulty.

twist.text: Watson famously answered 'Toronto' to a US cities clue. Even its failures were spectacular.

climax.text: Ken Jennings wrote on his answer: 'I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords.'

punchline.text: The computer won the game show. Humanity kept its sense of humor.

quiz.question: What was Watson's famous mistake during Jeopardy!?
options: It answered 'Toronto' to a US cities category clue
It refused to answer any questions
It crashed during the final round

details.summary: IBM's Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions in 2011, processing natural language clues to beat humans at a quiz requiring broad knowledge, wordplay, and cultural context.
details.whyItMatters: Watson showed AI could handle the messiness of human language — puns, idioms, and cultural references. It demonstrated practical natural language processing years before the LLM era.
takeaways: Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter
It processed natural language including wordplay and puns
The achievement demonstrated early NLP capabilities at scale

faq.question: How did Watson understand Jeopardy! clues?
faq.answer: Watson used a pipeline of over 100 NLP algorithms to parse clues, generate candidate answers, and rate their confidence. It processed the nuances of English puns and cultural references.

faq.question: What happened to Watson after Jeopardy!?
faq.answer: IBM pivoted Watson toward healthcare and business applications with mixed results. The technology struggled to deliver on commercial promises, though the Jeopardy demonstration remained a milestone in NLP history.
